answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1869–1948 · Indian independence leader & apostle of nonviolence
answer.sourceLine: Gandhi’s own words, in his own weekly. The sentence sits in The Doctrine of the Sword, Young India (Ahmedabad), 11 August 1920 — his reply to Indians urging armed revolt after Jallianwala Bagh. It follows “I do not believe myself to be a helpless creature… Let me not be misunderstood,” and is reprinted in the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, vol. 18. A stray Wikiquote talk-page note dating it to 1919 is why the line was long listed as unsourced; the real citation was on the same site all along.

source.excerpt: “I do not believe India to be helpless. I do not believe myself to be a helpless creature… Let me not be misunderstood. Strength does not come from physical capacity. It comes from an indomitable will.”
trail: Wikiquote’s Gandhi page ↗ carries the line in its sourced section, under the sub-heading ‘The Doctrine Of The Sword (1920)’, cited to Young India, 11 August 1920.

The full article is reproduced by the Bombay Sarvodaya Mandal at mkgandhi.org ↗, printed under the dateline ‘Young India, Ahmedabad, Wednesday, 11th August, 1920’. The sentence appears there verbatim, in the paragraph that continues “An average Zulu is any way more than a match for an average Englishman in bodily capacity…”
The same article is reprinted in the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, vol. 18, the volume covering 1 July to 17 November 1920, sourced there to Young India, 11-8-1920.

So why was it treated as unsourced for years? A note on the Wikiquote talk page ↗ pointed at Young India, volume 1, issue 52, 1919 — no article, no date, no page. That bad citation is still the one the aggregator sites copy, and it is a year off. The correct one was sitting in the sourced section of the same page.
source.excerptNote: The two-sentence form above is Gandhi’s own wording as printed in Young India. A compressed variant — ‘Strength does not come from physical capacity but from an indomitable will’ — circulates widely; it is a later smoothing of the primary text, not an independent version of it.
source.rightsNote: First published in Young India on 11 August 1920 — comfortably before the 1 January 1931 cut-off, so the text is in the public domain in the United States and free to reproduce. Keep the credit to Gandhi: that is courtesy and accuracy, not a licence condition.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: About Mahatma Gandhi
author.metaLine: 1869–1948 · Indian independence leader & apostle of nonviolence
author.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi led India’s independence movement through satyagraha — nonviolent civil resistance — and made a political method out of the claim that moral force outlasts physical force. He wrote constantly: his Collected Works run to roughly a hundred volumes, and he edited the weekly Young India for twelve years. That paper trail cuts both ways. It is why an unsourced Gandhi line deserves suspicion — and why a sourced one can be pinned down exactly, as this one is, to Young India of 11 August 1920 and volume 18 of the Collected Works.

misattribution.heading: The catch: a real quote with a wrong citation attached
misattribution.intro: The author was never in doubt, but the citation travelling with this line is. For years the sentence was passed around as an unsourced Gandhi-ism, or pinned to a 1919 reference that is a year off — while the actual article sat, correctly dated, in the sourced section of the same Wikiquote page.

items.why: Not a paraphrase and not a translation. The two sentences appear exactly as quoted in “The Doctrine of the Sword,” which Gandhi wrote in English for Young India, 11 August 1920, and which is reprinted in the Collected Works, vol. 18.

This is a Wikiquote talk-page note with no article, date or page — and the wrong year. Aggregator sites that give any citation at all copy this one. The correct reference is the issue of 11 August 1920.
The one-sentence run-on version is a smoothing of the printed text, not a variant reading. If you are quoting, use Gandhi’s two sentences.

misattribution.truthLine: Gandhi wrote it, in Young India on 11 August 1920. The only thing that was ever wrong here was the citation people carried with it.

context.heading: Why Gandhi wrote it
lead: The line compresses Gandhi’s central political wager because he wrote it to do exactly that. “The Doctrine of the Sword” was his answer, in August 1920, to Indians who had concluded after Jallianwala Bagh that only armed force would move the British. His reply was not that violence is impractical but that strength had been misidentified: “I do not believe India to be helpless. I do not believe myself to be a helpless creature.”

Then the sentence, and then the image that explains it — an average Zulu outmatches an average Englishman in bodily capacity and still flees an English boy, because he fears the boy’s revolver. The point is that the sword-holders are not strong; they are feared. Satyagraha — literally ‘holding firmly to truth’ — was the bet that a disciplined will, willing to absorb violence without returning it, outlasts that.
context.detailsSummary: Why this took so long to pin down
detailsBody: The sentence spent years being copied as an unsourced Gandhi-ism, or hung on a Wikiquote talk-page note citing Young India, volume 1, issue 52, 1919 — no article, no date, no page, and the wrong year. That is the reference the aggregator sites inherited.

The real one was never hidden. The same Wikiquote page lists the line in its sourced section under ‘The Doctrine Of The Sword (1920)’, the Bombay Sarvodaya Mandal reproduces the whole article under its 11 August 1920 dateline, and the Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi carry it in vol. 18. A bad citation is stickier than no citation: it looks like the work was already done.
